protocol.question: Does the stage-64 break-even inequality s/a > r - 1 predict which timed selection policies beat random, when decision cost r is varied from about 1.2 to 6.5?
protocol.data: ByteTransformer (35,776 parameters) and AdamW as in stages 58-64. UD r2.15 PADT and EWT prepared splits. Candidates from train. Probe: the stage-63 64-chunk dev sample (seed 6301), used only by reuse4. Target: 512 chunks drawn without replacement (seed 6501) from dev chunks that no model has scored, i.e. excluding the stage-49 sample (seed 4800, 128 chunks) and the stage-63 probe. Test splits are not read.
protocol.schedule: Per language/seed: 32 warmup batches of four train chunks, then a 20000-by-64 matrix of candidate indices, then 20000 uniform integers in [0,4). An arm with K candidates uses the first K columns of each row, so candidate sets are nested. Random applies column choice[step]. One common schedule and warmed state per language/seed, independent clones per run.
protocol.policies: random and reuse4: unchanged stage-58/60 decision functions inside the stage-58 deadline loop (experiments.pud_reuse.timed_run) on the first four columns. lossK: inside the same deadline loop with only the decision function replaced, clone model and optimizer, score the K candidates in one no-grad batched forward pass by mean next-byte cross-entropy, apply one AdamW update with the highest-loss candidate (first index wins ties).
protocol.order: Enumerate languages then seeds. In repeat j of state i, rotate the listed arms left by (i + j) modulo 5; five repeats place each arm once at each position.
protocol.timing: Single thread, deterministic Torch. Three seconds per run including indexing, cloning, scoring, probe refreshes and updates; only updates completed within the budget are accepted. Setup, warmup, schedule, initial clone, target evaluation and replay are outside the timer. Abort on nonfinite values, schedule exhaustion or missing cases. Write each run immediately.
protocol.primary: Arabic mean target loss (nats per byte transition) at the deadline, loss16 minus random. Average the five repeats within seed, then the ten seeds equally. Report a paired percentile bootstrap 95% interval over seeds. Negative favors loss16.
protocol.decomposition: For every guided run with n accepted updates, replay the first n random-schedule choices from the warmed state and evaluate. Per state and arm, with repeat means: r = random updates / arm updates; a = initial loss - loss of random at n; s = loss of random at n - arm loss; selection term -s; throughput term = random@n - random final. Report language means of r, s/a, both terms.
protocol.prediction_test: For each language, state and guided arm (2 x 10 x 4 = 80 cases), the inequality predicts the arm beats random in time iff s/a > r - 1. Report agreement between that prediction and the observed sign of (random final - arm final), as counts per arm and language, and the agreement rate. Descriptive; s and a are measured on the same runs, so this is a consistency check of the first-order approximation, not an independent forecast.
protocol.secondary: Same primary contrast in English. Each other guided arm minus random, and loss16 minus loss4, with the same interval method, labelled secondary. Updates and overruns per arm. No pooled cross-language effect, no multiplicity-adjusted claims, no adaptive change of K or budget.
protocol.coverage: 2 languages x 10 seeds x 5 arms x 5 repeats = 500 timed runs. Audit: summary recomputation from records, exact replay of every final loss from recorded choices, untimed replay of lossK and reuse4 decisions over each state's longest prefix, random-choice prefixes, deadline adherence, target disjointness from the stage-49 and stage-63 dev samples.
protocol.scope: Small byte-level model on one CPU host. The dev target is unscored but from the same corpus as the exposed splits. Cost ratios depend on hardware and batch shapes. The three-second clock is not total training cost.
